drills.q: Walk me through a forward pass of a GPT block, tensor shapes included.
drills.a: x:(B,T,C) -> LN -> QKV proj to (B,T,3C) -> split/reshape to (B,nh,T,hd) -> SDPA -> reshape back to (B,T,C) -> proj -> add residual -> LN -> MLP (C->4C->GELU->C) -> add residual.

drills.q: Why is weight tying between embedding and LM head not just a parameter-saving trick?
drills.a: Saves ~31% of GPT-2(124M) params, and empirically also slightly improves quality by forcing input/output token representations into a compatible space (Press & Wolf 2017).

drills.q: Derive why gradients vanish/explode more in deep post-norm transformers than pre-norm.
drills.a: Post-norm: x_{l+1}=LN(x_l+f(x_l)), gradient passes through L LayerNorm Jacobians compounding over depth. Pre-norm: x_{l+1}=x_l+f(LN(x_l)), residual path is unmodified by normalization end to end.

drills.q: Compute the compute budget for training GPT-2(124M) on 10B tokens using 6ND, and estimate wall-clock time on 8xA100.
drills.a: 6*1.24e8*1e10 ~= 7.4e18 FLOPs. At ~1.4e15 FLOP/s achievable on 8xA100, ~5300s ~= 90 minutes.

drills.q: Your loss goes to NaN at step 340. Debug it live.
drills.a: Check precision first (fp16 overflow vs bf16), then verify gradient clipping is actually applied, then inspect the batch at that step for a pathological input (very long repeated sequence).

drills.q: What does torch.compile actually buy you and what's the catch?
drills.a: ~2x throughput via kernel fusion and reduced Python dispatch overhead; first call compiles (slow), and variable input shapes trigger repeated recompilation that can silently kill throughput.

drills.q: Explain depth-scaled initialization (1/sqrt(2*n_layer)) and what breaks without it.
drills.a: Without it, residual stream variance grows roughly linearly with depth as each block adds unit-variance output; scaling each block's output projection keeps cumulative variance ~constant. Skipping it shows up as slower convergence and worse asymptotic loss, not necessarily NaN.

drills.q: A colleague says 'just double model size and tokens, it'll be strictly better.' True under fixed compute?
drills.a: No -- 6ND means doubling both roughly quadruples compute; within a fixed budget there's a loss-optimal ratio (Chinchilla-style), not simply 'more of everything'.

drills.q: Validation loss looks great but generated samples are repetitive and low quality. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check if this is a decoding artifact (greedy decoding on an undertrained model loops) vs a training problem -- compare measured perplexity against expected scaling-law value for the model's size/token budget before concluding training failed.

drills.q: Design a from-scratch nanoGPT build for someone with one consumer GPU and two evenings.
drills.a: Tier 1: char-level Shakespeare (minutes) to validate pipeline correctness (masking, target shift, loss, sampling). Tier 2: small subword model on a few hundred million tokens overnight, with compile/bf16/clipping/schedule present from the start.
